clinicalPearls: A late-onset mucocutaneous bleeding disorder from acquired loss of von Willebrand factor function, arising without a personal or family bleeding history
Bleeding is typically mucosal and cutaneous, with epistaxis, bruising, and gastrointestinal blood loss, sometimes from associated angiodysplasia
Classically associated with lymphoproliferative and plasma-cell disorders (paraprotein), myeloproliferative neoplasms, and high-shear cardiac lesions such as severe aortic stenosis
Heyde syndrome links severe aortic stenosis to loss of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers and gastrointestinal angiodysplasia bleeding
Laboratory findings mirror inherited von Willebrand disease with a disproportionately low von Willebrand factor activity relative to antigen and loss of high-molecular-weight multimers
Mechanisms include antibody-mediated clearance, adsorption onto malignant or platelet surfaces, and shear-induced proteolysis of multimers
Treatment is directed at the underlying cause, with von Willebrand factor-containing replacement or immunomodulatory measures used to control bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome develops when a previously normal von Willebrand factor system is disrupted by an underlying disorder. Autoantibodies may accelerate clearance or neutralise function, malignant cells or activated platelets may adsorb the protein, and high shear stress across stenotic valves or in myeloproliferative states can unfold von Willebrand factor and expose it to excessive proteolysis by ADAMTS13. The common consequence is selective loss of the largest, most haemostatically active multimers, impairing platelet adhesion and producing a bleeding phenotype resembling inherited von Willebrand disease.
additionalInvestigations: Von Willebrand factor activity (platelet-binding assay) and antigen with calculation of their ratio
Von Willebrand factor multimer analysis to demonstrate loss of high-molecular-weight forms
Factor VIII activity, which may be reduced in parallel
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein
Full blood count and marrow or clonality studies for lympho- or myeloproliferative disease
Echocardiography when a high-shear cardiac lesion such as aortic stenosis is suspected
redFlags: Major or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding, especially with suspected angiodysplasia
New mucocutaneous bleeding in a patient with a known paraprotein or myeloproliferative neoplasm
Bleeding with severe aortic stenosis suggesting Heyde syndrome
Bleeding refractory to standard replacement, implying rapid clearance
reference.prognosis: Outcome tracks the underlying disorder, and bleeding often resolves when that condition is treated, for example after valve replacement or control of a clonal disorder. Persistent or untreated causes can lead to recurrent and difficult-to-manage haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as new-onset inherited von Willebrand disease despite the late presentation
Failing to search for a paraprotein, myeloproliferative neoplasm, or aortic stenosis
Expecting a durable response to replacement when antibody-mediated clearance is rapid
Overlooking angiodysplasia as the bleeding source in Heyde syndrome
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
